doc.title: Josephine Davies interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 14, 2025

title: Making a living as a jazz musician in England; Ronnie Scott's and Instagram
summary: She says it has become harder, but she has curated a free life; venues like Ronnie Scott's judge social media following.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: If you talk to current jazz musicians here in the States about the state of jazz, it’s usually not an uplifting conversation. Over here we have -- academia keeps the music alive I think. That’s where it mostly lives. Or in the wealthy institutions. But club-wise it’s not a – in comparison to what – where are the good old days, I’m not sure which days they were. But I’m wondering about how hard is it to make a living as a jazz musician in England?

Yeah. It’s one of those questions that again it depends on the mood of the person speaking probably. I think it is hard. I think it has got harder. There is a sense sometimes of no one’s got any money and there are so many bands trying to get the same gigs and every year there are more bands. Most of them are fantastic. And there are fewer pubs and the pubs that there are lose their funding, and the travel around the U.K. is difficult, everything is expensive, traffic is horrendous, etcetera, etcetera. And so there is a reality to all of that. But I’m a big proponent of there is some positive, not in a bland, facile way, © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-

but a sense of how can I make the current world work for me. Because I think it’s always good to bear in mind that yes there are things that are more challenging, more difficult, and potentially terrible. But there are also things that have become better for a lot of people. And I think it’s important for me to remember that and feel that I am still living this incredibly creative, spontaneous, free life, which is extraordinary to have that and to be able to really do what I want on a daily basis. I mean I have made the decision I am – I don’t have a husband or children or animals or anything like that. So I have curated my life to be one in which I can have enough freedom and not have to worry too much about the difficulty of getting gigs. So there’ll always be something that I can do to make money. So for me it’s not so much about the financial aspect as just where would I like to play and it’s a struggle trying to get gigs at places like Ron Scott’s where I love playing Ronnie Scott’s and it’s very high profile and it’s a great venue, and incredibly hard to get a gig there. Because they look, as many venues do now, they look at your Instagram profile to see how many likes you have and how many followers. Things like that. Where you don’t really have a sense of control over that unless you are somebody that does social media on a daily basis and make it part of your job. Fair enough to the people who are doing that. I don’t really want to because of lots of reasons. I don’t really want to. But it does make it more difficult because they will literally say, “Well you can’t guarantee an audience.” And I’ll say, “Well no, I can’t.” So I don't know what needs to happen to sort of make things slightly easier. I think there are certain musicians for whom it is easier because they’ve got a higher profile, maybe they’re more – they’ve got a long history of having an audience. And then there was some newcomers who become quite high profile quite quickly. And then there’s the majority, the 98 percent of us in the middle who are going hmm, must I do another Instagram post if I want to get a gig at Ronnie Scott’s? Again I’m being slightly facetious but I’d say it is difficult. I’d say everyone would answer that question slightly differently, that it’s hard to know really. But I try and keep on keeping on, because I love what I do.
